cases.question: What happens if I retry a completed Mira task with the same identifier?

response.text:
According to the Mira queue notes, if you retry a completed task with the same identifier, it will return the stored result instead of creating another task. This is because the completed task's result is stored using its identifier. A different identifier, however, will create a new task.

[mira-queue.txt Page 1]

source_citations.text:
Mira is a fictional local queue demonstration. Every task has an owner, an identifier, and one of three states: pending, running, or complete. The demo has one worker, which starts the oldest pending task after the current task finishes. A completed task's result is stored using its identifier. Retrying the same identifier returns the stored result instead of creating another task. A different identifier creates a new task.

The notes define latency as the time from submission until completion.

ntifier creates a new task.

The notes define latency as the time from submission until completion. They explain why a slower worker can increase queue waiting time even when the submission endpoint responds quickly. They do not give measured request timings, percentile latency, throughput, a user count, or an experiment duration. The one-worker design is a teaching example; the notes do not claim it scales to a hosted multi-process service.

cases.question: If other conditions stay the same, what happens when Lumen aperture area decreases?

response.text: When the Lumen aperture area decreases, and other conditions stay the same, the rig admits less light to the sensor. This is because the aperture area determines how much light enters the sensor. A smaller aperture area means less light is admitted, which can be compensated for by increasing the exposure duration. [lumen-rig.txt Page 1]

source_citations.text:
Lumen is a fictional optics rig. An aperture admits light to a sensor. Reducing aperture area admits less light when other conditions stay the same. A longer exposure collects light for more time. The rig's sensor converts collected light into a recorded signal, and a dark frame is collected with the aperture covered. The example notes use the dark frame to identify a background signal.
